nodes.title: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
nodes.opening: Céline’s song is called On ne change pas —”we don’t change.” I think that’s both fortunately and unfortunately true for most of us. Fortunately in the sense that the sweet, innocent, curious, vivacious little one is still inside us, even if hiding. Unfortunate in the sense that we often don’t truly develop the adult qualities that we might pretend to have, so we continue burdening that little one inside us with troubles they aren’t made for handling. This shows up in how we may feel abandoned, helpless, impulsive, frightened, or desperate to be chosen.
nodes.ending: Reparenting isn’t an exercise you finish, after all. Feeling safe inside while you tell your boss no, or say what you really need, is the reparenting itself, whether or not a meditation ever made you cry. The sessions are practice for that.

nodes.title: Before You Try to Go Deep
nodes.opening: How much of the grown-up you is actually here right now? Try looking around the room, pausing before you act, making a choice and following through on it. If you can’t do that because you’re basically the frightened kid, leave the deeper conversation until later. You may need somebody steady there with you, or to do whatever helps you come back a bit before you try to talk to the child.
nodes.ending: As for when their little one gets a turn, I’d say once they’ve had some bad days where scaring somebody would’ve felt good, and they didn’t do it. Until then it helps a lot to have a real person in their life who likes them and won’t laugh along, since loving-kindness is easier to pick up from someone who already has some.

nodes.title: Your Body Might Need Some Love First
nodes.opening: If you notice tension in your solar plexus or abdomen, or anywhere else that seems to be keeping you from relaxing into that heart chakra love, try some non-forced, slower exhales and a little gentle self-massage. I love using one foot to massage the other foot like a yin-yang symbol, but you can start with some nice circular or spiral massage right on the tense spot.
nodes.ending: Bring the challenge back gradually, and only when you want to and you’re recovering well. Some people try to toughen themselves up in a cauldron, but what you’re looking for is the edge where you can actually learn. And what about those hard dreams, or images that pop up during a session? They can show what feels important or frightening right now. Sometimes they show what feels missing, or what feels needed. They aren’t evidence that what you saw in them happened, though, and shouldn’t be used to confirm a memory or rebuild one. Or to suggest one.

nodes.title: You Don’t Need an Inner Monologue
nodes.opening: If you don’t hear a little kid talking in your head, don’t invent one. Actually, this is one place where the usual inner-child prompt to “ask your little one what they need” can get confusing, because “ask” sounds like you’re supposed to ask a question and then wait for a second voice to answer. nodes.ending: And it might not be the same order all the time. You could have a feeling before thoughts, or thoughts might come first and provoke a feeling. They say hindsight is 20/20, but you actually might not even know which happened first. That’s ok, too.

nodes.title: Borrow One Competency at a Time
nodes.opening: A complete ideal parent may be impossible to imagine (unless you saw The Brady Bunch). And imagination is pretty hard for adults anyway since it kinda gets stamped out of kids at an early age, but it’s not just a foolish waste of time. It’s actually a genius mode unlock. So since the adult is actually a baby when it comes to power to imagine, start small: Borrow one function at a time from a figure who embodies it. Perhaps a therapist or your grandmother really cared for you. Perhaps your teacher at some age was a great guide. Maybe an older sibling protected you well. And there’s always your future healed self if you can imagine that.
nodes.ending: The thank-you you weren’t waiting for might not come anyway. 😜 More like “Oh, so NOW you care?” Which, fair enough, you did take a while. Your first instinct might be “But I’m trying!”, and then it’s just two six-year-olds arguing. Some days, just hearing it out like a decent adult is the only thing you’ll manage to borrow, and your little one might still roll their eyes at you. 🙄

nodes.title: Borrow Hindsight
nodes.opening: I sometimes ask: “How would I respond to this once I understood it more clearly, in balance and with compassion?” It’s a question borrowed from your future self. It can change how the whole thing looks. It can also just make you feel a bit more like that person, or less alone (sometimes all at once). Keep in mind it’s only their best guess. No perfect Higher Self is handing down answers.
nodes.ending: You can borrow a wiser future version of whoever else is involved, too, as long as you don’t assume they’ll end up on your side, or sorry. What the current one keeps doing is still what you go by, however good the picture looks (the future one has never called you back).

nodes.title: Remember When You Already Did It
nodes.opening: My father often suggested folks remember a similar-level (or even harder) challenge that they were able to handle. Maybe you survived a car crash and surgery a few years ago, but now you’re having trouble with emotional eating. You can draw strength from the past. As my sister, a historian, likes to say, “The past didn’t go anywhere.” Your own challenge doesn’t need to be as dramatic as a car crash, as long as it really happened. So who or what helped you get through it? Is one piece of that still within reach? If you catch yourself thinking “I survived a car crash, so why can’t I stop eating when I’m upset?”, that’s the past turned into a stick to hit yourself with. Maybe you’re more worn out now, or missing whatever helped back then. (No example? Try another doorway.)

nodes.title: Notice the Part That Came Here
nodes.opening: Some people hear all this about love and answer, “No. I hate myself.” If that’s what you find, it deserves an honest hearing. Just listen to it, without arguing back. But if you opened this article, something in you wanted things to be different, whatever the rest of you was saying. The same goes if you came to therapy or asked someone for help. Or maybe you’d already decided you were hopeless, and then for some reason you tried again.
nodes.ending: What was it? It might have been hope, or desperation. Maybe you were curious, or scared. Some people come here out of duty. Or it was more like, “I’m not going to keep suffering like this.” And maybe it was love. You don’t need to decide which. Ask that part what it hoped might happen when it brought you here, and follow that thread.

nodes.title: Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
nodes.opening: Sometimes it’s not that you can’t love in general. Your dog can chew up your good shoes and be forgiven before you’ve found the other one. But maybe you direct that love to your little one and the attempt goes flat, or starts to feel weirdly unsafe. Just feel that love you can feel for others for a minute, in your body, before you try to redirect anything. Then as you relax into that and enjoy it more, imagine it flowing downhill, like an overflowing river of delicious chocolate. Now imagine how happy your inner child is at the bottom of the hill to play in that chocolate love that rolled down!
nodes.ending: This goodwill isn’t just for the target of it, though. You may find it bounces back and opens up a little warmth in your heart. And if “I love you” goes flat when you aim it at yourself or your little one, the same wish works there, too. 🫶🏿

nodes.opening: Set one boundary. “What’s a ‘boundary’?”, I might be asking. That looks like saying no to something that’s costing you too much (money, time, whatever it is). nodes.ending: After the day, look at what actually happened. If you did the Protector action(s), not feeling better right away is information to learn from. It doesn’t mean failure. nodes.title: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over
nodes.opening: Pema Chödrön calls the tightening and urge you get before the story has finished forming “shenpa,” and she says “ hooked “ is a more descriptive translation than the usual “attachment.” You might notice the hook before you have any clue what part of you is doing the hooking. Or you might notice it embarrassingly late. The jaw and stomach are already tight, and/or half the text is written, and then suddenly it dawns on you: you’re supposed to be observing yourself. 😀 Maybe forget the parts detective work for a minute. You can figure that out later.
nodes.ending: The opposite extreme of our pendulum, throwing everything transient away, as some people do with “thought-noting” practice, also isn’t healthy, except as a meditation exercise. Transient feelings and thoughts can be meaningful signals. For example, if you don’t want to be touched, say no now and work out what it means later. Same if something might be dangerous right now, or might be a medical warning sign: step away or get checked first.

nodes.title: A Heart-to-Child Loop
nodes.opening: With a little warmth to work with, rest one hand at the center of your chest (the heart chakra) and feel for love, and the other on the solar plexus, just below, and feel for your little one. The solar plexus is the most vulnerable part of the torso. One punch there hurts a lot, as I sadly learned while getting beaten up every day at kindergarten recess by a gang organized by my best friend. Can you believe it? So it makes sense to look for your little one there.
nodes.ending: Picture the love traveling from your heart down to your little one. If some comes back up, let it, and send it on down again, so it goes around like a loop. That part’s a gift from them, and they don’t owe it to you, so if nothing comes back, just keep sending yours. No warmth today? Then rest your hands there and notice what you find, no faking required. Non-judgement is a place to start. It can blossom into love over time.

nodes.title: Journal With Each Hand
nodes.opening: Lucia Capacchione, an art therapist, wrote a whole book on this one, The Power of Your Other Hand . As titles go, it’s pretty literal. Your other hand, the clumsy one, writes like a first grader anyway, so it gets the scared or hurt feelings (nothing made up). The usual hand answers, as the grown-up. Some people who get nothing but silence from their little one are surprised by what the other hand comes up with. A protective part might grab the pen first, and then it gets that hand until it’s had its say.
nodes.ending: And what if all that writing leaves you more confused than when you started? Then just keep track for a while, and save the patterns for later, if they turn out to matter at all. A memory aid doesn’t have to explain your life. It could be a dated note of what happened, or of what helped. A reminder or a next step works too. Or you can leave yourself a voice note.

nodes.title: Just Like Me
nodes.opening: This one works best on a steadier day, when thinking about other people won’t pull you out of your own shoes. Name the feeling plainly. Lonely, say. Then think of how many people are feeling that exact thing right now, and wanting it to stop, just like you. With that many people feeling the same thing, the theory that you’re the defective one gets kind of hard to keep up. Some of them make it worse trying to get away from it. Just like you, sometimes. 😅 Wish all of you, you first, enough support to stay with it, so the pain stops with you.
nodes.ending: If you’ve tried Pema Chödrön’s tonglen , this is a gentler cousin, and normal breathing is fine. Whoever hurt you might come to mind, too. Forgiving them isn’t part of it, and neither is picturing their childhood. Getting in touch is a separate decision, for a much calmer day, if it ever comes.

nodes.title: “And So That’s the Way It Happened!”
nodes.opening: My ex, Xandria, taught me to append “And so that’s the way it happened!” to a difficult memory. Say it the way a grandpa would finish a story on the porch. (”Once upon a time…” helps if the start is where you get stuck.) Somehow it moves the whole thing out of the courtroom, where the case was still being argued, and into your life story. Pick a memory you can handle for the first few tries.
nodes.ending: Do keep an ear on who’s narrating, though. If the voice starts sneering, like it’s making fun of the younger you, stop right there (that’s the courtroom creeping back in). Same if you feel more ashamed, or kind of floaty and unreal, since more distance won’t help with that. And when it goes well, it’s a good time to check in with the younger you in that story. What do they need from you now?

nodes.title: Use Childhood Photographs Gently
nodes.opening: Maybe you’ve tried picturing your little one and thought, “This feels fake. I’m just making it up.” A real photo of you as a child can help with that, since there’s no face or posture to invent. Yes, yes, it might feel a bit strange, seeing your own face from back then. nodes.ending: Put the photo back in its drawer when you’re finished. Settle yourself in the present to close out properly. Re-evaluation counseling always ends on this “Present Time” reminder. Can be as simple and silly as “Oh, Today is Monday, my favorite day of the week!”

nodes.opening: A lot of people get stuck right here. nodes.title: The Parent You Inherited
nodes.opening: I’d look at the parent “script” you inherited: how you learned to treat yourself from how people treated you growing up, long before you started building your Nurturer, Protector and Guide. It can be warm, but it’s often more like a critic, or a warden with rules. The rules can even sound reasonable, like “You can come back to the table when you’re done with your embarrassing crying fit.” If yours was like that, your little one learned bit by bit to hide that part of their authentic self which wasn’t allowed, so they could keep belonging. They might still be doing it.
nodes.ending: But with the borrowed adulthood trick, the new grown-up can start outside your head, as someone who likes you the way you are, or as something you do to protect your little one, like letting the phone ring when you know how that call goes. You don’t have to pretend to feel anything to let a phone ring. Your little one can watch you do it many times before trusting you, while the parent you inherited calls it fake.

It can be warm, but it’s often more like a critic, or a warden with rules. The rules can even sound reasonable, like “You can come back to the table when you’re done with your embarrassing crying fit.” If yours was like that, your little one learned bit by bit to hide that part of their authentic self which wasn’t allowed, so they could keep belonging. They might still be doing it.
old.ending: But with the borrowed adulthood trick, the new grown-up can start outside your head, as someone who likes you the way you are, or as something you do to protect your little one, like letting the phone ring when you know how that call goes. You don’t have to pretend to feel anything to let a phone ring. Your little one can watch you do it many times before trusting you, while the parent you inherited calls it fake.

nodes.title: Two Common Protective Patterns
nodes.opening: Two kinds of reaction really are trying to protect you, more often than not. The first one is on duty all the time, and it can sound like a skeptic: “You’re just making this up.” It may have spent years keeping you from being humiliated again, or left again. That’s a long time to stay on guard. It might be tired by now, but it’s experienced and good at what it does. It has probably watched you get excited about other healing things, then drop them.
nodes.ending: The other one shows up when you get close to something painful, as a sudden pull to do anything but feel it (even a yawn can come with an “I’m so done with this” feeling). It might believe there’s no grown-up around who could hold what’s coming up. I’d want out too. That yawn might actually be the opposite of checking out, though. Re-evaluation Counseling, a kind of peer counseling, counts yawning as emotional discharge, a feeling on its way out. The skeptic and the pull both started out trying to prevent something that really hurt, and they can keep at it even when what they do now hurts you. If you treat either one like an enemy, or like proof that something’s wrong with you, it’ll probably just think “See? I knew it,” and stay in charge. I wonder what it would do if it didn’t have to.

nodes.title: Hear the Protective Part First
nodes.opening: Whichever protective part showed up, try talking to it in the same Nurturer voice you meant for your little one. A harder voice can seem more fitting for something that’s been in your way. I’d still keep it the same. If that voice isn’t there in you yet, borrow it from someone who’s been safe for you. At some point you can ask that part, “What are you afraid would happen if you stepped back?” It might say this will just be one more performance, and you’ll fool yourself again.
nodes.ending: Taking the hostility out makes room for warmth. What people most often say helped is letting their defenses down. I mean by choice, after the part guarding you has been heard. If you’ve never been safe being loved, your ego can act like a rigid security guard that won’t let the feeling in, and being vulnerable is the opening the feeling needs. (This guard is only about letting the feeling in. People still have to earn your trust.) Sometimes the warmth is there, with a cold part standing in front of it, guarding something. That part tends to step aside once it’s been heard.

nodes.title: When to Change the Strategy
nodes.opening: Weeks in and nothing much is changing? I’d want to quit too, or else keep doing the exact same thing forever so I never had to find out. Before either one, I’d look for what exactly is in the way. Sometimes those weeks were mostly reading about it and getting ready, which can feel a lot like doing it (this article included). Or you did sit down with your little one, and fear got there first, or a part of you that’s trying to protect you. It can be as plain as never having the place to yourself. Whatever it turns out to be, I’d work on that one thing instead of giving up on everything.
nodes.ending: Don’t be afraid to ask your therapist/yourself “What is this practice supposed to help, and how would I know if it’s helping?” This sovereign, gently curious stance should apply to everything in life. Feeling calmer or having deeper insights or explanations for the trauma response are some possible signs of initial progress, but if that’s the endgame, it’s just a cope. Real healing is ultimately measured by reduced need for the therapy. It’s like real parenting: you might start out reading parenting books and thinking hard about what to say or do, but after a while you get into the groove and a lot of it becomes natural. Inner parenting can be like that too. You don’t need to keep checking this guide or planning every conversation with your little one; the nurturing, protecting and guiding become more automatic. You might still turn to therapy when you need it, and life will keep offering chances to grow wiser and more compassionate. And if the therapy is actually working, it should improve your daily life, and especially the health of the inner child-inner adult relationship. Going at it harder isn’t as useful as going at it with more wisdom and compassion. Take the parts that work, and innovate on the rest.

nodes.title: Sometimes There Isn’t a Clear Child Yet
nodes.opening: Reparenting assumes there’s a clear little one in there to love, and for a lot of people there is. But if you grew up somewhere you only belonged as long as you played somebody else, like a really controlling family or a strict church, the real one may never have had room to form. All this stuff about your little one could have left you wondering who I’m even talking about.
nodes.ending: Give a new interest enough tries to get past the humiliation of being a beginner, when you keep telling people, “Sorry, I’m new.” Maybe after that you still genuinely dislike it, and then you may quit. You may also discover a part of yourself that never had permission to exist. Either way, that’s pl/ork in its most literal form: play becomes part of forming your identity. You might catch yourself wondering when you became someone who does this.

nodes.title: From Survival to Experimental Play
nodes.opening: If your childhood meant avoiding pain and keeping the people you needed close, your attention got used up reading danger (was that sigh about me?) and meeting their expectations, and when curiosity or mistakes got you punished, or it felt like they loved you less, you got better at the part. That left much less room for experiments that show you what you like when nobody’s grading you. People grow into who they are by trying things on and then changing their minds, from what they wear down to the ideas and roles they take up, like a teenager who starts spelling her name with an “i” at the end and later changes it back.
nodes.ending: So early on, the practice is finding out who’s actually in there, through long reflection with no outside input, and journaling just for yourself, without picturing a reader. You might catch yourself explaining who everybody is anyway. Time alone in nature helps too, and so does getting back the preferences that got buried: the foods you really like and what feels good to do, and what you believe and feel when nobody’s around to take your cues from. Focusing (Eugene Gendlin’s method of listening to a vague, felt sense in your body) can especially help you notice feelings and preferences the part you’ve been playing learned to overlook. Any words you put to them can stay tentative (”I hate cooking... or just for everybody?”) while you look at what they seem to mean and revise how you read them.

nodes.title: Untangling the Belonging Bargains
nodes.opening: Part of building who you are is untangling yourself from whatever pulls you away from your own knowing in return for belonging. A political tribe might expect consistent positions and predictable reactions, while a family or religion that’s kind to you might have expectations that just feel like being good. Most groups expect some conformity, which is ordinary. Your family might want a particular kind of son or daughter, and your friends might have rules about what you can joke about or get upset about. But if going along means betraying yourself, that’s the bargain.
nodes.ending: Key developed this identity and differentiation portion of the method, drawing on Murray Bowen’s family-systems work and her own self-therapy.

nodes.title: Four Pairs That Commonly Hook the Child
nodes.opening: Pema Chödrön has a quick map for finding the bargain. It’s four pairs, starting with pleasure and pain, and gain and loss. The other two are about what people think of you: praise and blame, and good reputation and disgrace. Your little one can panic when something hurts, and also when something good might disappear, like praise, romance, money, status, belonging or a spiritual high. You might still be enjoying one of those when your little one starts asking how long this is going to last.

nodes.title: The Inner Guide
nodes.opening: As the Guide, you choose what your little one learns and what it gets to experience, and you hold standards, the way a good parent would. You ask hard things of it so it can grow, at its own pace. That’s what I was just asking of you, with that new interest. nodes.title: How Much Happiness Do You Know Is Possible?
nodes.opening: What do you picture when you wish someone well? Probably them fed and safe, with people around who like them, stuff like that. Wanting that for somebody is love (babies get this part already), and practical love matters a lot. The horizon of what I can wish for someone is partly shaped by the happiness, peace, and freedom I know are possible.
nodes.ending: It feels like you’re connecting with your little one, but the contact is staying near the surface. Meditating for a long time and then sleeping can open up much more emotionally direct stuff, especially in a second sleep, after you’ve already slept once. What showed me that the daytime pl/ork had stayed shallow was the difference at night. So say you wake up from a dream with far more feeling and need in it than the session came anywhere near. That’s the sign this is you (a session that was good and just didn’t stick around is something else). Then ask what that dream let you feel that the session didn’t, and how you understand it now. And if nightmares start wrecking your sleep, do less of the practice, earlier in the day or for a shorter time, before you write off the whole thing.

nodes.title: Somatic Heart Opening
nodes.opening: Rumi says you have to keep breaking your heart until it stays open. Some people find that deep grieving gives way to warmth, or to feeling connected. Some feel held, in the body. Being loved can open grief from the other side, too. Someone takes care of you, and you think, “Why does this make me sad?” It can be sadness for the care that was missing, and that doesn’t mean the love failed. While you’re present and still choosing, stay with it. Crying that deep can overwhelm you, too. It can retraumatize, mostly when nobody’s with you or you’ve disappeared into the sadness. Once it’s swamping you instead of opening you, slow down (like turning the song off for the night).

nodes.title: When the Practice Feels Real but Stays Shallow
nodes.opening: It feels like you’re connecting with your little one, but the contact is staying near the surface. Meditating for a long time and then sleeping can open up much more emotionally direct stuff, especially in a second sleep, after you’ve already slept once. What showed me that the daytime pl/ork had stayed shallow was the difference at night. So say you wake up from a dream with far more feeling and need in it than the session came anywhere near. That’s the sign this is you (a session that was good and just didn’t stick around is something else). Then ask what that dream let you feel that the session didn’t, and how you understand it now. And if nightmares start wrecking your sleep, do less of the practice, earlier in the day or for a shorter time, before you write off the whole thing.

nodes.title: Borrowed Adulthood in Relationship
nodes.opening: Reparenting is usually talked about as something you do alone, or with a therapist. But your little one got hurt in relationships, and that kind of hurt can only heal so far on your own. Sometimes one person ends up doing a lot of the borrowed grown-up jobs at once. They cook, they keep track of the appointments, they drive, they’re the one who says it’ll be okay, or they’re just the competent person in the room. Maybe you’re picturing them right now. Having someone like that while you’re struggling can be an enormous blessing.
nodes.ending: This is part of why I connect inner-child pl/ork with Hearthwork and with building community. Having a beautiful experience on the inside isn’t really the point. The love has to move, and it doesn’t always go the same way round (the door you came in through matters less than the loop). From a spiritual experience to your little one, then into your relationship with the grown-up you, then out to other people, and back again.

nodes.title: First Social Connections, Done Right
nodes.opening: Then there are people you’re just getting to know. Meeting them can turn into a kind of test--”First impressions are everything,” as they say, but it could be even worse than that, if you need them to prove you’re lovable. Nobody’s a reassurance machine. I’m giving you permission now to quit school and flunk the tests. Get curious about who this person is, and who you are, and let both of you have your own reasons for being there in the beautiful present. Leaning on each other is still a big part of relationships, and it goes both ways. In a real crisis, getting a safe person involved can be exactly the right move.
nodes.ending: So I’d ask them, before handing over any tricky specifics: “What does the law require you to report?” That's a normal and expected question. Although personally I wouldn't even bother with that. You can always rephrase things as a dream narrative to get the emotional content across without triggering alarm bells (although I actually got in trouble with TalkSpace therapy bot even for a dream!). Just don’t hold back a danger that’s happening now from people who can help, and get anyone in danger safe before worrying about the rest. Sometimes telling on yourself is the thing that keeps someone safe, whatever it costs you legally.

nodes.title: Other Folks Also Have Hooks
nodes.opening: Once you’re in your happy place, look at the other person too, and don’t go only by the one fight where they crossed your boundary, or, the other way around, by the one “no” or boundary of theirs that made you mad — after all, they’re allowed to say no to you. nodes.title: Speak Toward What You Are Building
nodes.opening: It’s not so hard to understand that words have power. They point your attention somewhere, so aim them at what you want more of, whether that’s something you’d like to be able to do or a relationship. Say you tell yourself “I’m not dependent.” Well, now you’re thinking about being dependent. Being totally independent also isn’t realistic nor ideal, and can even seem like just a reaction to the original problem. We can often strike a nice nuanced poetic balance, like: “I’m provided for by the universe, like the birds & lilies Jesus reminded us of.” With your little one, and in hypnosis especially, make it easy to picture: warmth, protection, steadiness, rest, whatever’s really needed to melt into your happy place. You’ll save a ton of money on vacations!
nodes.ending: What they tell you is worth remembering, too, until they say something different. (And don’t guess it from their gender or some other stereotype.) Same with advice you’ve already given: if nothing new has changed it, a quick “like I said” and moving on works better than offering it again like it’s new.

nodes.title: How to Forgive Without Forgetting
nodes.opening: For many people, healing does get around to some forgiveness eventually, or at least to not being run by the resentment anymore. It can’t be put on a schedule (nobody gets a gold star for forgiving fastest). And you don’t have to forgive first to get safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable, get justice or get better. Then again, active resentment narrows what you see, and your little one stays organized around the injury. And if someone pressures you into forgiving early, what you get is an enlightened-looking act, with the wound gone underground.
nodes.ending: Forgiving yourself works the same way. Own what you did (only what was yours), and let yourself feel the remorse. Repair what you can, by apologizing or making amends. Changing the behavior counts too. Then you’re allowed to stop holding yourself hostage, and the responsibility stays. If you’re thinking “not me, not after what I did,” forgiving other people tends to be harder too. Some harms take years, so don’t push it. Forgive too soon and it’s only a show; stay in the resentment and you end up living there. Every so often, come back to how whoever did it got to be someone who could do that, until you understand it well enough that it changes how you feel.

nodes.title: When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn’t Begun
nodes.opening: Your little one can get really loud in the gap after one life ends and before the next one has formed. A breakup will do it, or moving to another country, an illness, losing your faith or a role, your youngest moving out. So can leaving a family or community, or staying in one on new terms. Tibetan Buddhism calls an in-between state a bardo . You don’t have to buy what it teaches about death and rebirth to use the everyday part: endings leave a stretch where the old you is gone and the new one hasn’t shown up.
nodes.ending: All of this happens in you, so it doesn’t matter whether they get any of it (nobody’s checking their inbox). It doesn’t stand in for grieving, though, or for getting in touch when that’s right, and your boundaries still apply. Same with the practical stuff. And if it starts making you more compulsive, or a bit unreal, so you can’t get back to your life, make it simpler: “I miss you, and I care.” Some of that same care can go to the part of you that’s still here.

nodes.purpose: Keep transitions, grief and uncertainty as their own application.

nodes.title: How This Relates to Schema Therapy
nodes.opening: Of the clinical approaches I know, schema therapy is the closest to this guide. Its therapists do what they call limited reparenting : within professional limits, they give you some of what a good parent would, with warmth and firmness and some playfulness too. Over time you take that in, and it becomes your own “Healthy Adult,” who looks after your “Vulnerable Child” and stands up to the punishing parent in your head. Sound familiar? That’s a Nurturer and a Protector by other names, and since the therapist’s version becomes yours bit by bit, it’s borrowed adulthood too.
nodes.ending: Where it really differs is spirituality. Schema therapy leaves it out. That’s not so surprising, since it grew out of cognitive therapy ( Jeffrey Young , who developed it, did his postdoctoral work with Aaron Beck). So a loan of love from God, like back in Ask God for a Loan, isn’t something a schema therapist would usually offer you. IFS goes overboard the other way, in my opinion (more on that in the next section). Past that, a lot depends on who you’re seeing.

old_nodes.title: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
old_nodes.opening: Céline’s song is called On ne change pas —”we don’t change.” I think that’s both fortunately and unfortunately true for most of us. Fortunately in the sense that the sweet, innocent, curious, vivacious little one is still inside us, even if hiding. Unfortunate in the sense that we often don’t truly develop the adult qualities that we might pretend to have, so we continue burdening that little one inside us with troubles they aren’t made for handling. This shows up in how we may feel abandoned, helpless, impulsive, frightened, or desperate to be chosen.
old_nodes.ending: Reparenting isn’t an exercise you finish, after all. Feeling safe inside while you tell your boss no, or say what you really need, is the reparenting itself, whether or not a meditation ever made you cry. The sessions are practice for that.

old_nodes.title: Don’t Give the Inner Adult Away
old_nodes.opening: If you still feel like a kid inside, somebody who seems grown-up can feel like salvation, and letting them do some of the grown-up jobs for you can actually help for a while. But they can know things you don’t and still be wrong about you. The test is whether the relationship makes me more grounded, truthful, and free.

old_nodes.title: Before You Try to Go Deep
old_nodes.opening: How much of the grown-up you is actually here right now? Try looking around the room, pausing before you act, making a choice and following through on it. If you can’t do that because you’re basically the frightened kid, leave the deeper conversation until later. You may need somebody steady there with you, or to do whatever helps you come back a bit before you try to talk to the child.
old_nodes.ending: As for when their little one gets a turn, I’d say once they’ve had some bad days where scaring somebody would’ve felt good, and they didn’t do it. Until then it helps a lot to have a real person in their life who likes them and won’t laugh along, since loving-kindness is easier to pick up from someone who already has some.

old_nodes.title: Your Body Might Need Some Love First
old_nodes.opening: If you notice tension in your solar plexus or abdomen, or anywhere else that seems to be keeping you from relaxing into that heart chakra love, try some non-forced, slower exhales and a little gentle self-massage. I love using one foot to massage the other foot like a yin-yang symbol, but you can start with some nice circular or spiral massage right on the tense spot.
old_nodes.ending: Bring the challenge back gradually, and only when you want to and you’re recovering well. Some people try to toughen themselves up in a cauldron, but what you’re looking for is the edge where you can actually learn. And what about those hard dreams, or images that pop up during a session? They can show what feels important or frightening right now. Sometimes they show what feels missing, or what feels needed. They aren’t evidence that what you saw in them happened, though, and shouldn’t be used to confirm a memory or rebuild one. Or to suggest one.

old_nodes.title: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over
old_nodes.opening: Pema Chödrön calls the tightening and urge you get before the story has finished forming “shenpa,” and she says “ hooked “ is a more descriptive translation than the usual “attachment.” You might notice the hook before you have any clue what part of you is doing the hooking. Or you might notice it embarrassingly late. The jaw and stomach are already tight, and/or half the text is written, and then suddenly it dawns on you: you’re supposed to be observing yourself. 😀 Maybe forget the parts detective work for a minute. You can figure that out later.
old_nodes.ending: You can mean the apology for a start. Then notice what happens next. Are you sorry for what you did, or are you starting to take back the complaint too because they’re still upset? Maybe your first explanation sucked. Try again. 😅 And if it fails again, and you’ve said what you mean, well, you can’t guarantee they’ll understand it. Guilt may keep shouting at you. That doesn’t tell you the whole conflict was your fault, nor does it prove they’re manipulating you.

old_nodes.title: Other Folks Also Have Hooks
old_nodes.opening: Once you’re in your happy place, look at the other person too, and don’t go only by the one fight where they crossed your boundary, or, the other way around, by the one “no” or boundary of theirs that made you mad — after all, they’re allowed to say no to you. Does it keep ending the same way, where you bring up something that hurt and then still end up reassuring them they’re not a bad person, and the talk never comes back to what happened to you? (The psychologist Lindsay Gibson wrote the book on this: Disentangling from Emotionally Immature People .) Or can they hear you disagree and look at their own part?

Maybe your first explanation sucked. Try again. 😅 And if it fails again, and you’ve said what you mean, well, you can’t guarantee they’ll understand it. Guilt may keep shouting at you. old_nodes.title: First Social Connections, Done Right
old_nodes.opening: Then there are people you’re just getting to know. Meeting them can turn into a kind of test--”First impressions are everything,” as they say, but it could be even worse than that, if you need them to prove you’re lovable. Nobody’s a reassurance machine. I’m giving you permission now to quit school and flunk the tests. Get curious about who this person is, and who you are, and let both of you have your own reasons for being there in the beautiful present. Leaning on each other is still a big part of relationships, and it goes both ways. In a real crisis, getting a safe person involved can be exactly the right move.
old_nodes.ending: It’s also how your voice sounds, though. You can say all the right words, but if the tone is accusatory, it doesn’t matter.

old_nodes.purpose: Preserve the explicit no: connection is part of the care, not a reward for completing this reading route.

old_nodes.title: Opening up honestly to the right people at the right pace
old_nodes.opening: And reaching out doesn’t mean telling strangers everything. Privacy isn’t fakery. People can earn more of you by how they handle the smaller stuff, like whether that thing you told them about your weird fear of birds turns into a joke at the next party 🙈, and how they take it when you say no. But if a relationship is getting deep and you’re still keeping up a fake normal, happy version of yourself to hold onto it, I’d either bring more of the truth in, carefully, or let it be less deep for now. (If telling could put you in real danger, like violence, or being outed where that isn’t safe, protect yourself first.) And when someone finally accepts you, it can feel amazing. It still doesn’t prove you’re meant for each other, or that they’ve earned your trust yet.
old_nodes.ending: So I’d ask them, before handing over any tricky specifics: “What does the law require you to report?” That's a normal and expected question. Although personally I wouldn't even bother with that. You can always rephrase things as a dream narrative to get the emotional content across without triggering alarm bells (although I actually got in trouble with TalkSpace therapy bot even for a dream!). Just don’t hold back a danger that’s happening now from people who can help, and get anyone in danger safe before worrying about the rest. Sometimes telling on yourself is the thing that keeps someone safe, whatever it costs you legally.

old_nodes.opening: Noticing Counts
old_nodes.ending: Say a friend sits with you while you fall apart. Most of us feel better and call them again the next time, and they get a little better at it every time while we don’t. old_nodes.title: Borrow One Competency at a Time
old_nodes.opening: A complete ideal parent may be impossible to imagine (unless you saw The Brady Bunch). And imagination is pretty hard for adults anyway since it kinda gets stamped out of kids at an early age, but it’s not just a foolish waste of time. It’s actually a genius mode unlock. So since the adult is actually a baby when it comes to power to imagine, start small: Borrow one function at a time from a figure who embodies it. Perhaps a therapist or your grandmother really cared for you. Perhaps your teacher at some age was a great guide. Maybe an older sibling protected you well. And there’s always your future healed self if you can imagine that.
old_nodes.ending: The thank-you you weren’t waiting for might not come anyway. 😜 More like “Oh, so NOW you care?” Which, fair enough, you did take a while. Your first instinct might be “But I’m trying!”, and then it’s just two six-year-olds arguing. Some days, just hearing it out like a decent adult is the only thing you’ll manage to borrow, and your little one might still roll their eyes at you. 🙄

old_nodes.title: Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
old_nodes.opening: Sometimes it’s not that you can’t love in general. Your dog can chew up your good shoes and be forgiven before you’ve found the other one. But maybe you direct that love to your little one and the attempt goes flat, or starts to feel weirdly unsafe. Just feel that love you can feel for others for a minute, in your body, before you try to redirect anything. Then as you relax into that and enjoy it more, imagine it flowing downhill, like an overflowing river of delicious chocolate. Now imagine how happy your inner child is at the bottom of the hill to play in that chocolate love that rolled down!
old_nodes.ending: Being the grown-up doesn’t mean controlling everything yourself, though. After a betrayal like that, part of you might want to. Spiritual support can help you act where it’s yours to act, and let go of outcomes and other people’s choices where it isn’t. The Serenity Prayer is the example I’d give, if prayer still feels like yours.

old_nodes.title: A Smaller Doorway: Goodwill
old_nodes.opening: Sometimes “I love you” is more than you can honestly say, especially to somebody who’s treated you badly. Even the usual whittled-down loving-kindness prayer, “May you be happy,” can feel like rewarding them. That’s why I go with Buddha’s overall wish (paraphrasing): “May you be loving, peaceful, and free,” since if they were all of those, they wouldn’t have done what they did, and then they actually would be lovable.
old_nodes.ending: This goodwill isn’t just for the target of it, though. You may find it bounces back and opens up a little warmth in your heart. And if “I love you” goes flat when you aim it at yourself or your little one, the same wish works there, too. 🫶🏿

old_nodes.title: Not Every Hero Wears A Cape
old_nodes.opening: Set one boundary. “What’s a ‘boundary’?”, I might be asking. That looks like saying no to something that’s costing you too much (money, time, whatever it is). Handle that task you’ve been putting off, or the tax man, or your DUIs in Maryland, even if all you do today is open the envelope. Keep one small promise to your little one. Clean your room! old_nodes.title: The Parent You Inherited
old_nodes.opening: I’d look at the parent “script” you inherited: how you learned to treat yourself from how people treated you growing up, long before you started building your Nurturer, Protector and Guide. It can be warm, but it’s often more like a critic, or a warden with rules. The rules can even sound reasonable, like “You can come back to the table when you’re done with your embarrassing crying fit.” If yours was like that, your little one learned bit by bit to hide that part of their authentic self which wasn’t allowed, so they could keep belonging. They might still be doing it.
old_nodes.ending: But with the borrowed adulthood trick, the new grown-up can start outside your head, as someone who likes you the way you are, or as something you do to protect your little one, like letting the phone ring when you know how that call goes. You don’t have to pretend to feel anything to let a phone ring. Your little one can watch you do it many times before trusting you, while the parent you inherited calls it fake.

old_nodes.title: Two Common Protective Patterns
old_nodes.opening: Two kinds of reaction really are trying to protect you, more often than not. The first one is on duty all the time, and it can sound like a skeptic: “You’re just making this up.” It may have spent years keeping you from being humiliated again, or left again. That’s a long time to stay on guard. It might be tired by now, but it’s experienced and good at what it does. It has probably watched you get excited about other healing things, then drop them.
old_nodes.ending: The other one shows up when you get close to something painful, as a sudden pull to do anything but feel it (even a yawn can come with an “I’m so done with this” feeling). It might believe there’s no grown-up around who could hold what’s coming up. I’d want out too. That yawn might actually be the opposite of checking out, though. Re-evaluation Counseling, a kind of peer counseling, counts yawning as emotional discharge, a feeling on its way out. The skeptic and the pull both started out trying to prevent something that really hurt, and they can keep at it even when what they do now hurts you. If you treat either one like an enemy, or like proof that something’s wrong with you, it’ll probably just think “See? I knew it,” and stay in charge. I wonder what it would do if it didn’t have to.

A harder voice can seem more fitting for something that’s been in your way. I’d still keep it the same. If that voice isn’t there in you yet, borrow it from someone who’s been safe for you. At some point you can ask that part, “What are you afraid would happen if you stepped back?” It might say this will just be one more performance, and you’ll fool yourself again.
old_nodes.ending: That part doesn’t have to move out. It’s been living there way longer than the grown-up you. It can keep watch while you take one small step toward your little one, and I think watching is what it wants anyway, to find out if there’s a grown-up here now who could call it off if things got to be too much. If it says no, I’d listen. When it lets you, keep an eye on that part too, for any change at all. If it’s been calling all this stupid, it might turn out to be scared of getting its hopes up. I wouldn’t want to get mine up either. I’d tell it something like, “You don’t have to hope yet, I’ll keep coming back even when I mess up.” Sometimes it doesn’t say anything back for a while.

old_nodes.title: When to Change the Strategy
old_nodes.opening: Weeks in and nothing much is changing? I’d want to quit too, or else keep doing the exact same thing forever so I never had to find out. Before either one, I’d look for what exactly is in the way. Sometimes those weeks were mostly reading about it and getting ready, which can feel a lot like doing it (this article included). Or you did sit down with your little one, and fear got there first, or a part of you that’s trying to protect you. It can be as plain as never having the place to yourself. Whatever it turns out to be, I’d work on that one thing instead of giving up on everything.
old_nodes.ending: Sometimes the session itself goes really well. You feel real care for your little one and say exactly what they needed to hear. And a few days later you’re skipping lunch and saying yes to everything again. A lot of people’s first guess is that they didn’t go deep enough. I don’t think that’s it, though, and I don’t think this one failed either. Maybe the grown-up just hasn’t come out of the exercise with you yet. Whatever you did for your little one in there, I’d try a tiny bit of it out here, like texting a friend that you’re having a rough day instead of saying you’re fine. That can honestly be harder than the meditation was. One small thing like that can teach your little one more than ten more good meditations. It doesn’t have to happen after every session.

old_nodes.title: From Survival to Experimental Play
old_nodes.opening: If your childhood meant avoiding pain and keeping the people you needed close, your attention got used up reading danger (was that sigh about me?) and meeting their expectations, and when curiosity or mistakes got you punished, or it felt like they loved you less, you got better at the part. That left much less room for experiments that show you what you like when nobody’s grading you. People grow into who they are by trying things on and then changing their minds, from what they wear down to the ideas and roles they take up, like a teenager who starts spelling her name with an “i” at the end and later changes it back.
old_nodes.ending: So early on, the practice is finding out who’s actually in there, through long reflection with no outside input, and journaling just for yourself, without picturing a reader. You might catch yourself explaining who everybody is anyway. Time alone in nature helps too, and so does getting back the preferences that got buried: the foods you really like and what feels good to do, and what you believe and feel when nobody’s around to take your cues from. Focusing (Eugene Gendlin’s method of listening to a vague, felt sense in your body) can especially help you notice feelings and preferences the part you’ve been playing learned to overlook. Any words you put to them can stay tentative (”I hate cooking... or just for everybody?”) while you look at what they seem to mean and revise how you read them.

old_nodes.title: A Heart-to-Child Loop
old_nodes.opening: With a little warmth to work with, rest one hand at the center of your chest (the heart chakra) and feel for love, and the other on the solar plexus, just below, and feel for your little one. The solar plexus is the most vulnerable part of the torso. One punch there hurts a lot, as I sadly learned while getting beaten up every day at kindergarten recess by a gang organized by my best friend. Can you believe it? So it makes sense to look for your little one there.
old_nodes.ending: Picture the love traveling from your heart down to your little one. If some comes back up, let it, and send it on down again, so it goes around like a loop. That part’s a gift from them, and they don’t owe it to you, so if nothing comes back, just keep sending yours. No warmth today? Then rest your hands there and notice what you find, no faking required. Non-judgement is a place to start. It can blossom into love over time.

old_nodes.opening: If you weren’t loved well as a child, “love your inner child” can sound like nonsense. Love them how? Maybe you really want the best for your little one. Maybe you hug them in your imagination, or miss them. And you can still feel none of the warmth people mean when they say love. That doesn’t close the door, though, it just means you start smaller.
old_nodes.ending: Curiosity can be enough here, something like “Other people say they’ve felt a depth of love or peace that I never have. I don’t know if I believe their explanation. But what if the experience is possible for me?” Don’t assume the limits of what you’ve felt so far are the limits of what’s possible.

old_nodes.title: Notice the Part That Came Here
old_nodes.opening: Some people hear all this about love and answer, “No. I hate myself.” If that’s what you find, it deserves an honest hearing. Just listen to it, without arguing back. But if you opened this article, something in you wanted things to be different, whatever the rest of you was saying. The same goes if you came to therapy or asked someone for help. Or maybe you’d already decided you were hopeless, and then for some reason you tried again.
old_nodes.ending: What was it? It might have been hope, or desperation. Maybe you were curious, or scared. Some people come here out of duty. Or it was more like, “I’m not going to keep suffering like this.” And maybe it was love. You don’t need to decide which. Ask that part what it hoped might happen when it brought you here, and follow that thread.

old_nodes.title: Somatic Heart Opening
old_nodes.opening: Rumi says you have to keep breaking your heart until it stays open. Some people find that deep grieving gives way to warmth, or to feeling connected. Some feel held, in the body. Being loved can open grief from the other side, too. Someone takes care of you, and you think, “Why does this make me sad?” It can be sadness for the care that was missing, and that doesn’t mean the love failed. While you’re present and still choosing, stay with it. Crying that deep can overwhelm you, too. It can retraumatize, mostly when nobody’s with you or you’ve disappeared into the sadness. Once it’s swamping you instead of opening you, slow down (like turning the song off for the night).

old_nodes.title: How Much Happiness Do You Know Is Possible?
old_nodes.opening: What do you picture when you wish someone well? Probably them fed and safe, with people around who like them, stuff like that. Wanting that for somebody is love (babies get this part already), and practical love matters a lot. The horizon of what I can wish for someone is partly shaped by the happiness, peace, and freedom I know are possible.

old_nodes.title: When the Practice Feels Real but Stays Shallow
old_nodes.opening: Some people have the opposite problem. It feels like you’re connecting with your little one, but the contact is staying near the surface. Meditating for a long time and then sleeping can open up much more emotionally direct stuff, especially in a second sleep, after you’ve already slept once. What showed me that the daytime pl/ork had stayed shallow was the difference at night. So say you wake up from a dream with far more feeling and need in it than the session came anywhere near. That’s the sign this is you (a session that was good and just didn’t stick around is something else). Then ask what that dream let you feel that the session didn’t, and how you understand it now. And if nightmares start wrecking your sleep, do less of the practice, earlier in the day or for a shorter time, before you write off the whole thing.

old_nodes.title: How to Forgive Without Forgetting
old_nodes.opening: For many people, healing does get around to some forgiveness eventually, or at least to not being run by the resentment anymore. It can’t be put on a schedule (nobody gets a gold star for forgiving fastest). And you don’t have to forgive first to get safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable, get justice or get better. Then again, active resentment narrows what you see, and your little one stays organized around the injury. And if someone pressures you into forgiving early, what you get is an enlightened-looking act, with the wound gone underground.
old_nodes.ending: Forgiving yourself works the same way. Own what you did (only what was yours), and let yourself feel the remorse. Repair what you can, by apologizing or making amends. Changing the behavior counts too. Then you’re allowed to stop holding yourself hostage, and the responsibility stays. If you’re thinking “not me, not after what I did,” forgiving other people tends to be harder too. Some harms take years, so don’t push it. Forgive too soon and it’s only a show; stay in the resentment and you end up living there. Every so often, come back to how whoever did it got to be someone who could do that, until you understand it well enough that it changes how you feel.

old_nodes.title: When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn’t Begun
old_nodes.opening: Your little one can get really loud in the gap after one life ends and before the next one has formed. A breakup will do it, or moving to another country, an illness, losing your faith or a role, your youngest moving out. So can leaving a family or community, or staying in one on new terms. Tibetan Buddhism calls an in-between state a bardo . You don’t have to buy what it teaches about death and rebirth to use the everyday part: endings leave a stretch where the old you is gone and the new one hasn’t shown up.
old_nodes.ending: All of this happens in you, so it doesn’t matter whether they get any of it (nobody’s checking their inbox). It doesn’t stand in for grieving, though, or for getting in touch when that’s right, and your boundaries still apply. Same with the practical stuff. And if it starts making you more compulsive, or a bit unreal, so you can’t get back to your life, make it simpler: “I miss you, and I care.” Some of that same care can go to the part of you that’s still here.

old_nodes.title: Borrowed Adulthood in Relationship
old_nodes.opening: Reparenting is usually talked about as something you do alone, or with a therapist. But your little one got hurt in relationships, and that kind of hurt can only heal so far on your own. Sometimes one person ends up doing a lot of the borrowed grown-up jobs at once. They cook, they keep track of the appointments, they drive, they’re the one who says it’ll be okay, or they’re just the competent person in the room. Maybe you’re picturing them right now. Having someone like that while you’re struggling can be an enormous blessing.
old_nodes.ending: Maybe you’d rather that your support person were a lover, as well. Lots of people open a dating app in the middle of the night, hoping someone will make it all stop hurting. 🙈 If that’s you right now, dating can wait while your friends and the steady people around you do their part. That doesn’t mean you have to be completely healed before you date, but when romance should follow when two people really love each other and want to build a life together. It won’t rescue you from the pain or reward you for healing, and it sucks to mess up a beautiful relationship because of unhealed trauma, believe me, I know. I wrote a whole romance guide , mostly due to this.

old_nodes.title: Speak Toward What You Are Building
old_nodes.opening: It’s not so hard to understand that words have power. They point your attention somewhere, so aim them at what you want more of, whether that’s something you’d like to be able to do or a relationship. Say you tell yourself “I’m not dependent.” Well, now you’re thinking about being dependent. Being totally independent also isn’t realistic nor ideal, and can even seem like just a reaction to the original problem. We can often strike a nice nuanced poetic balance, like: “I’m provided for by the universe, like the birds & lilies Jesus reminded us of.” With your little one, and in hypnosis especially, make it easy to picture: warmth, protection, steadiness, rest, whatever’s really needed to melt into your happy place. You’ll save a ton of money on vacations!
old_nodes.ending: This is part of why I connect inner-child pl/ork with Hearthwork and with building community. Having a beautiful experience on the inside isn’t really the point. The love has to move, and it doesn’t always go the same way round (the door you came in through matters less than the loop). From a spiritual experience to your little one, then into your relationship with the grown-up you, then out to other people, and back again.

old_nodes.title: You Are Worthy of Love. Always.
old_nodes.opening: It’s the same love as back in Your Loan is PRE-APPROVED!, the Divine Love that can start as a little spark of … something when you give thanks. That kind, whether you’d say it comes from God or the universe itself or whatever, was there before you could earn anything. Love from a person is more conditional than that. Somebody’s love running out on you still says nothing about what you’re worth.
old_nodes.ending: Be patient with yourself, and gentle, including with the part of you that thinks you should be over it by now. You are more than your pain and your past. That’s easy to lose sight of when you’ve spent so long looking at them. And you aren’t alone. There’s help, and lots of other people are out there learning to look after their own little ones.

old_nodes.title: Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood
old_nodes.opening: We all need some support, especially when taking our first steps. First and easiest is to start with finding a somatic therapist, if that resonates, as per my Somatic Therapies Guide .
old_nodes.ending: Regarding AI therapy, I’ve tried all the top AI therapy apps, and they’re all pretty bad. I’m trying to make my own based on this guide, but I’m becoming more convinced that unsupervised AI therapy is just a toss up. That doesn’t mean you can’t get a lot of great insights sometimes when talking to AI, though, but just expect it to go sideways sometimes.

old_nodes.title: How This Relates to Schema Therapy
old_nodes.opening: Of the clinical approaches I know, schema therapy is the closest to this guide. Its therapists do what they call limited reparenting : within professional limits, they give you some of what a good parent would, with warmth and firmness and some playfulness too. Over time you take that in, and it becomes your own “Healthy Adult,” who looks after your “Vulnerable Child” and stands up to the punishing parent in your head. Sound familiar? That’s a Nurturer and a Protector by other names, and since the therapist’s version becomes yours bit by bit, it’s borrowed adulthood too.
old_nodes.ending: Where it really differs is spirituality. Schema therapy leaves it out. That’s not so surprising, since it grew out of cognitive therapy ( Jeffrey Young , who developed it, did his postdoctoral work with Aaron Beck). So a loan of love from God, like back in Ask God for a Loan, isn’t something a schema therapist would usually offer you. IFS goes overboard the other way, in my opinion (more on that in the next section). Past that, a lot depends on who you’re seeing.

old_nodes.title: How This Relates to IFS
old_nodes.opening: Richard Schwartz, who developed Internal Family Systems (IFS), called one of his books No Bad Parts . Honor, understand and love every part, he says, and the protective ones are no exception, so “meet the protector first” would fit right in over there. That’s a lot of the overlap with this method, right there in the title.
old_nodes.ending: And the parts just keep coming: managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, new subparts... At some point it’s a maze, with a little one somewhere in the middle of it. A gentle practitioner can walk you through it fine. With others, people seem to come out more fragmented than they went in. Having a big institute with certifications behind it doesn’t make a model any truer, either. Or safer, for that matter.

Old site

All of this happens in you, so it doesn’t matter whether they get any of it (nobody’s checking their inbox). It doesn’t stand in for grieving, though, or for getting in touch when that’s right, and your boundaries still apply. Same with the practical stuff. And if it starts making you more compulsive, or a bit unreal, so you can’t get back to your life, make it simpler: “I miss you, and I care.” Some of that same care can go to the part of you that’s still here.
Borrowed Adulthood in Relationship
Reparenting is usually talked about as something you do alone, or with a therapist. But your little one got hurt in relationships, and that kind of hurt can only heal so far on your own. Sometimes one person ends up doing a lot of the borrowed grown-up jobs at once. They cook, they keep track of the appointments, they drive, they’re the one who says it’ll be okay, or they’re just the competent person in the room. Maybe you’re picturing them right now. Having someone like that while you’re struggling can be an enormous blessing.

First Social Connections, Done Right

Old site

You can mean the apology for a start. Then notice what happens next. Are you sorry for what you did, or are you starting to take back the complaint too because they’re still upset? Maybe your first explanation sucked. Try again. 😅 And if it fails again, and you’ve said what you mean, well, you can’t guarantee they’ll understand it. Guilt may keep shouting at you. That doesn’t tell you the whole conflict was your fault, nor does it prove they’re manipulating you.
First Social Connections, Done Right
Then there are people you’re just getting to know. Meeting them can turn into a kind of test--”First impressions are everything,” as they say, but it could be even worse than that, if you need them to prove you’re lovable. Nobody’s a reassurance machine. I’m giving you permission now to quit school and flunk the tests. Get curious about who this person is, and who you are, and let both of you have your own reasons for being there in the beautiful present. Leaning on each other is still a big part of relationships, and it goes both ways. In a real crisis, getting a safe person involved can be exactly the right move.
Source context

New site

Maybe you’d rather that your support person were a lover, as well. Lots of people open a dating app in the middle of the night, hoping someone will make it all stop hurting. 🙈 If that’s you right now, dating can wait while your friends and the steady people around you do their part. That doesn’t mean you have to be completely healed before you date, but romance should follow when two people really love each other and want to build a life together. It won’t rescue you from the pain or reward you for healing, and it sucks to mess up a beautiful relationship because of unhealed trauma, believe me, I know. I wrote a whole romance guide , mostly due to this.

Other Folks Also Have Hooks

Old site

The opposite extreme of our pendulum, throwing everything transient away, as some people do with “thought-noting” practice, also isn’t healthy, except as a meditation exercise. Transient feelings and thoughts can be meaningful signals. For example, if you don’t want to be touched, say no now and work out what it means later. Same if something might be dangerous right now, or might be a medical warning sign: step away or get checked first.
Other Folks Also Have Hooks
Once you’re in your happy place, look at the other person too, and don’t go only by the one fight where they crossed your boundary, or, the other way around, by the one “no” or boundary of theirs that made you mad — after all, they’re allowed to say no to you. Does it keep ending the same way, where you bring up something that hurt and then still end up reassuring them they’re not a bad person, and the talk never comes back to what happened to you? (The psychologist Lindsay Gibson wrote the book on this: Disentangling from Emotionally Immature People .) Or can they hear you disagree and look at their own part?
Source context

New site

So I’d ask them, before handing over any tricky specifics: “What does the law require you to report?” That's a normal and expected question. Although personally I wouldn't even bother with that. You can always rephrase things as a dream narrative to get the emotional content across without triggering alarm bells (although I actually got in trouble with TalkSpace therapy bot even for a dream!). Just don’t hold back a danger that’s happening now from people who can help, and get anyone in danger safe before worrying about the rest. Sometimes telling on yourself is the thing that keeps someone safe, whatever it costs you legally.

Hearthwork: Taking Turns

Old site


(No source heading)
New navigation, not moved source wording

New site

What they tell you is worth remembering, too, until they say something different. (And don’t guess it from their gender or some other stereotype.) Same with advice you’ve already given: if nothing new has changed it, a quick “like I said” and moving on works better than offering it again like it’s new.
Hearthwork: Taking Turns
The basic premise of Hearthwork , my peer-counseling framework, is: Equal time. Attention without interpretation, advice, or fixing. You speak. I listen. Then we switch. Presence, Warmth, Discipline, Confidentiality. It’s kind of a third type of relationship, alongside ordinary friendship and professional therapy, and one your little one might really need, because modern life rarely gives you anything like it.

Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

Old site

Like MDMA, San Pedro is more protective and nurturing than many other medicines, especially at lower doses, so you don’t need as much Nurturer and Protector built up for those, though you still need some. Some people benefit more from solo therapy, while others benefit more from having a trained therapist guide the experience.
Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy
I’d learn to do inner-child therapy sober first, in your ordinary mindstate, since that’s the one you’ll be living in. Cars don’t start at 60mph, that’s not the way the universe seems to work. First gear leads to second leads to third, etc. Second gear, in this case, may refer to gentle meditation or self-hypnosis. When you’re ready, my self-hypnosis guide and lucid-dreaming guide can take those deeper, into third gear. Low doses of entheogens can also synergize compatibly with various gears: cactus, CBD tea with sublingual mapacho, Loveyhuasca , iboga , and so on.

Physical Pain Makes It Harder

Old site

Out of hundreds of times I’ve taken iboga, there was one time just a small amount of male iboga root bark got me a bit hypomanic, to the point where a thought came: “Everyone should listen to me!” Luckily I was trained in Buddhist meditation, so I immediately challenged it with “Why should anyone listen if they have no interest?” I stopped using iboga for a while after that, and I warn people about that potential issue with male iboga specifically.
Physical Pain Makes It Harder
Physical pain can bring on the urge to escape too. Say an attack has you curled up on the bathroom floor, and whatever knocked the pain out last time (say, fent, or ketamine) starts looking real good, though you know it’ll leave you worse if you keep resorting to that quick fix.

If You Want to Kill Yourself

Old site

Being ready to do anything to end the pain isn’t a suicide plan, so I wouldn’t present it as one to get relief. But if you’re scared you’ll actually hurt yourself, or can’t tell whether you’re safe, get someone with you right away.
If You Want to Kill Yourself
I try not to proselytize about spirituality, because I’ve made that mistake before, and I now see that it’s better to let folks find it when they are ready. But when someone tells me they want to kill themself, I consider the topic to be brutally opened by default, regardless of whether they meant to do that, because if they actually do kill their body (which they might mistake to be their self), that’s a very powerful spiritual challenge right there, even if they didn’t realize it would be.

If You Want to Kill Yourself
Maybe you’re reading this about to act, or with the means close by. Then before anything else, get another human being involved, and put some distance between you and the means. A crisis line or an emergency number counts, and the person on the other end can be a total stranger. Do the same if you can’t stop yourself, or you’re badly disoriented or intoxicated. Can’t tell if that’s you? Treat it like it is. None of that is me answering whether life is worth living. It just keeps the question open long enough to look at.

Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood

Old site

Be patient with yourself, and gentle, including with the part of you that thinks you should be over it by now. You are more than your pain and your past. That’s easy to lose sight of when you’ve spent so long looking at them. And you aren’t alone. There’s help, and lots of other people are out there learning to look after their own little ones.
Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood
We all need some support, especially when taking our first steps. First and easiest is to start with finding a somatic therapist, if that resonates, as per my Somatic Therapies Guide .

As I mentioned in my nibbana article , I’ve had my most profound spiritual peak experiences and realizations when I had the least interest in continued existence. And the Buddha taught in MN 129 , attaining a human birth is as rare and precious as it would be for a one-eyed turtle to pop his head up through a hoop on the surface of the vast ocean. You won the cosmic jackpot, so don’t throw away the ticket before you open the envelope to find it!

You Are Worthy of Love. Always.

Old site

This is part of why I connect inner-child pl/ork with Hearthwork and with building community. Having a beautiful experience on the inside isn’t really the point. The love has to move, and it doesn’t always go the same way round (the door you came in through matters less than the loop). From a spiritual experience to your little one, then into your relationship with the grown-up you, then out to other people, and back again.
You Are Worthy of Love. Always.
It’s the same love as back in Your Loan is PRE-APPROVED!, the Divine Love that can start as a little spark of … something when you give thanks. That kind, whether you’d say it comes from God or the universe itself or whatever, was there before you could earn anything. Love from a person is more conditional than that. Somebody’s love running out on you still says nothing about what you’re worth.

I’m trying to make my own based on this guide, but I’m becoming more convinced that unsupervised AI therapy is just a toss up. That doesn’t mean you can’t get a lot of great insights sometimes when talking to AI, though, but just expect it to go sideways sometimes.

excerpts.text: How Much Happiness Do You Know Is Possible?

One practical door anyone can use to slowly experience divine love is gratitude (even after the Turkey’s done & Thanksgiving is over!). Genuinely cultivated gratitude (not just empty/forced ritual) is one way to experience divine love for the first time, or to get it back when the feeling fades. I think it’s essential if we want to live in that love instead of occasionally visiting it.

Once you start to feel that lovely softness of the heart, invite your little one in with you as your spiritual integration practice. They might go numb, or call BS on that. If so, they might just need to see if you’re actually humble enough, and grateful enough for them, to listen to their rejection and be patient. If you instead retreat back into your cozy corner, it’s the food bank feast all over again: You can have an enormous spiritual feast upstairs while the child is still starving downstairs.
